questions.question: What does a Ruby interview cover and why does it exist? It assesses your grasp of Ruby's object model (everything is an object, blocks, mixins) and the Rails ecosystem — the skills a Ruby shop needs before hiring you.
questions.title: Ruby Interview Overview
questions.direct_answer: A Ruby interview evaluates your understanding of Ruby's object model (everything is an object, classes are objects, blocks/procs/lambdas, mixins via modules) and the Rails ecosystem, at the level the role demands. It exists because Ruby is expressive and opinionated — its object model, its 'blocks are everywhere' idiom, and Rails' convention-over-configuration shape how production code is written — and an interviewer must verify you've internalized those before hiring you to write Ruby/Rails. The interview typically spans the language core (objects, blocks, modules, metaprogramming), Rails (MVC, ActiveRecord, routing), testing (RSpec), and production concerns.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what a Ruby interview uniquely tests — the object model (everything is an object, blocks/procs/lambdas), mixins via modules, and the Rails convention-over-configuration ecosystem — not just Ruby syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a Ruby interview as a generic backend interview — missing blocks, the object model, module mixins, and Rails conventions that the interview actually probes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame the Ruby interview as testing the object model (everything is an object, blocks/procs/lambdas), mixins (modules over inheritance), and Rails (convention over configuration, ActiveRecord, MVC) — plus RSpec.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: A Ruby interview evaluates your understanding of Ruby's object model and the Rails ecosystem at the level the role demands. It exists because Ruby is expressive and opinionated — its object model, its 'blocks are everywhere' idiom, and Rails' convention-over-configuration shape how production code is written — and an interviewer must verify you've internalized those before hiring you. The interview typically spans the language core (everything is an object, blocks/procs/lambdas, modules as mixins, metaprogramming), Rails (MVC, ActiveRecord, routing, conventions), testing (RSpec), and production concerns (Sidekiq, deployment).

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas a Ruby interview tests: (1) the object model — everything is an object, including classes (a class is an instance of Class); every object has a class and a singleton class for per-object methods; (2) blocks, procs, lambdas — blocks are the ubiquitous idiom (each, map, with); procs and lambdas are callable objects you store; the difference is argument strictness and return behavior; (3) modules as mixins — Ruby has single inheritance but modules (include, prepend, extend) compose behavior, which is how shared behavior is wired; (4) metaprogramming — define_method, method_missing, class macros; (5) Rails — convention over configuration, ActiveRecord (the ORM that is the model layer), MVC, routing; (6) testing with RSpec (describe/it, let, expect).

sections.title: What a Ruby Interview Tests vs a Generic Backend Interview
rows: Objects everywhere, classes are objects, single inheritance + module mixins

sections.title: The object model, a block, and a mixin — Ruby idioms
sections.content:
# (1) EVERYTHING IS AN OBJECT, including classes.
"hello".class            # => String
String.class             # => Class   (a class is an instance of Class)
5.times { |i| puts i }   # even integers have methods; the { ... } is a BLOCK.

# (2) BLOCKS are the ubiquitous callable idiom.
[1,2,3].map { |n| n * n }   # => [1, 4, 9]   (block passed to map)
[1,2,3].each { |n| puts n }
#   A block is an anonymous chunk of code passed to a method. Procs and
#   lambdas turn a block into a stored object:
double = ->(x) { x * 2 }    # a lambda
double.call(5)              # => 10

# (3) MODULES AS MIXINS (single inheritance + composition).
module Loggable
  def log(msg) puts "[#{self.class}] #{msg}"; end
end
class Order
  include Loggable           # Order instances now have #log
end
Order.new.log("created")    # => [Order] created

sections.title: Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is Ruby's flexibility versus discipline: Ruby's openness (metaprogramming, monkey-patching, method_missing) is powerful but can produce code that's hard to trace and maintain; the interview tests whether you use the power judiciously. A second tension: Rails' convention over configuration is productive but opaque ('magic'); interviewers check whether you can trace what a convention actually does (which route maps to which controller action). The third: blocks/procs/lambdas are the signature Ruby idiom — confusing their differences (argument strictness, return behavior) is a common gap.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A Ruby interview tests the object model (everything is an object, classes are objects, single inheritance + module mixins), blocks/procs/lambdas, and the Rails ecosystem.
Blocks are the ubiquitous callable idiom (each, map, with); procs and lambdas are stored callables with different argument and return behavior.
Ruby has single inheritance; modules (include/extend) compose behavior as mixins — the primary sharing mechanism.
Rails' convention over configuration is productive but opaque; interviewers check you can trace what a convention does.
Metaprogramming (define_method, method_missing) is powerful but a discipline test — the interview probes judicious use.
RSpec (describe/it, let, expect) is the testing standard; the interview may check fixtures, doubles, and specs.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A Ruby interview evaluates your understanding of Ruby's object model and the Rails ecosystem at the level the role demands. It exists because Ruby is expressive and opinionated — its object model, its blocks-are-everywhere idiom, and Rails' convention-over-configuration shape how production code is written. The object model I anchor on is that everything is an object, including classes — a class is an instance of Class — and Ruby has single inheritance with modules as mixins, which is the primary way behavior is composed. Blocks are the ubiquitous callable idiom — each, map, and with all take a block — and procs and lambdas turn a block into a stored callable, with differences in argument strictness and return behavior that interviewers check. Rails is convention over configuration, which is productive but opaque, so interviewers check whether you can trace what a convention actually does, like which route maps to which controller action. The honest tension is Ruby's flexibility versus discipline: metaprogramming, monkey-patching, and method_missing are powerful but can produce code that's hard to trace, so the interview tests whether you use that power judiciously.
